plain_title: When ejaculation takes far too long, or doesn't come
one_liner: Marked delay or absence of ejaculation during partnered sex despite wanting it, for six months or more.
in_simple_words: Delayed ejaculation is when a person keeps taking much longer than they'd like to ejaculate during sex with a partner, or can't at all, even though they want to and have enough stimulation. It lasts at least six months and causes distress. Causes include medicines (especially some antidepressants), nerve conditions, diabetes, hormones, ageing, anxiety, relationship problems, and a gap between solo and partnered sex. A doctor checks medical and medicine causes. Sex therapy helps with the rest.
what_it_can_feel_like: People think it must be great to last forever. It's exhausting, and my partner thought it meant I wasn't attracted to her.
It turned out to be my antidepressant. My doctor switched it and the problem eased within weeks.
common_signs: Ejaculation takes much longer than wanted during partnered sex, or doesn't happen
Despite wanting to and having enough stimulation
Lasting at least six months, most of the time
Upset, frustration, tiredness, or soreness; a worried partner

myths_vs_facts.myth: Taking a long time is always a good thing.
myths_vs_facts.fact: When it's unwanted, it causes frustration, pain, and relationship strain. It's a real difficulty, not a bonus.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It means you're not attracted to your partner.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Medication, nerves, hormones, anxiety, and habits of stimulation are far more common causes than attraction.

how_common.plain: Delayed ejaculation affects about 1 to 4 in 100 men. It's more common with age and with some antidepressants. Many never report it.
how_common.figure: About 1%–3% (narrative review); up to 4% in some estimates

what_helps.plain_summary: The first step is a check of your health and your medicines. Antidepressants and some other drugs are a common cause, and a doctor may change them. Sex therapy works on anxiety, pressure to perform, and the gap between solo and partnered sex. It can include your partner. Medical treatments have limited evidence. Some medicines are used off-label, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Treating depression or relationship strain helps.
evidence_based_options: Medication and medical review by a doctor
Treatment of depression, anxiety, or relationship distress
Specialist referral for hormonal or neurological causes
self_help_that_supports_care: Noting when it started and any medication changes
Talking with your partner so it's not misread as rejection
Asking a doctor before stopping any medication

when_to_reach_out: If delayed ejaculation is causing distress or affecting your relationship, or it started after a medication change, talk to a doctor. Don't stop prescribed medication on your own.
is_not: Sexual difficulties that are occasional, explained by a medical condition or medication, caused by severe relationship distress, or that don't bother you aren't diagnosed as a disorder. Taking longer after drinking, when tired, or with age is common. It isn't a disorder unless it bothers you.
hope_note: When the cause is found, often a medication, things frequently improve. Therapy helps couples reconnect in the meantime.

content_notes: Sex-positive, shame-free wording; no explicit technique descriptions. Medication named only in general terms.
